rationale: Basal ganglia and autonomic mini-review cites historical salivation comparisons and gland treatment in Parkinson disease. The discussion gives symptom context without an original oral-fig comparison.
Rats developed transient visible drooling after cerebral artery occlusion. The report measures stroke-related neurological disability and ordinary food intake during recovery.
Pompe disease guideline describes pooling of saliva, tongue weakness, and feeding difficulty in affected infants. It gives a different disease and outcome mechanism.
Swallowing anatomy review separates chewing and saliva softening food from lip closure and actual drooling. Illustrations show normal and disordered anatomy without assigning fig.
Manganism historical review describes salivation among findings after manganese exposure. Case histories involve occupational toxicity rather than a raw fig exposure.

Postmortem Parkinson and Lewy body comparisons evaluate pathological signals in salivary glands and lower esophagus. Discussion distinguishes accumulated saliva from its production. No prospective drooling measure or fig intervention.

Supplementary video description identifies drooling in a case of genetic early-onset parkinsonism. It also distinguishes dysphagia in affected relatives. The clinical comparisons involve genotype and medication.
The case table records drooling among features of one chronic traumatic encephalopathy and motor-neuron-disease presentation. Illustrated tissue findings are unrelated to eating fig.

Figure 2 compares protein concentrations in unstimulated saliva for 24 Parkinson participants and 25 controls. The comparisons were inconclusive and the study did not measure graded drooling or test a fruit.
The phenotype table reports drooling occurrence by TCF4 deletion status. It concerns a chromosomal syndrome and compares genotype groups, with no dietary exposure.
Review of central cholinergic analgesia lists sialorrhea among drug adverse effects. It discusses cholinergic agents and their mechanisms without a raw fig intervention.
Sequencing of twins with dopa-responsive dystonia led to a medicine adjustment. The observed clinical changes follow the adjusted regimen without a raw fig comparator.
The case table documents drooling in two of five adults with Dravet syndrome and distinguishes other motor signs. The clinical histories give a different illness and no fig intervention.
An apraxia report describes unilateral drooling during the first week after a stroke. The figure depicts the lesion and the improvement description contains no dietary comparison.

A MAPT variant case history records drooling during a progressive akinetic-rigid presentation and later dysphagia. Clinical presentation initially prompted a Parkinson diagnosis. No graded fig response.
The case addresses intestinal pseudo-obstruction after brainstem hemorrhage. Its scan and procedure context differs from a fig and Parkinson drooling comparison.
The Angelman syndrome review lists frequent drooling and feeding problems as diagnostic context. It describes separate developmental and genetic features rather than a fig comparison.
Parkinson motor-control review lists drooling in Table 1 and discusses swallowing frequency and facial control as contributors. No independent dietary or salivation comparison is presented.
ALS management survey explicitly excludes sialorrhea from its analyzed care modalities. It does not test a raw-fig comparison.
Dystonia genetics review uses figures to summarize genes, pathways and phenotype relationships. It gives no comparison assigning fresh figs to a Parkinson population.
Postoperative dysphagia review discusses oral weakness, saliva handling and postsurgical causes after cervical spine surgery. Figures and general food transport do not establish studied fig exposure.
The Parkinson psychosis review lists sialorrhea among clozapine adverse effects. Its medication safety discussion is different from a fig and drooling response.
Review centers on molecular and clinical effects of levodopa, including motor complications. Its figures and nonmotor background do not supply a named raw fig exposure.
Neurological N-acetylcysteine review describes drooling in different syndrome case literature. It covers a drug and other neurological populations without an oral-fig comparison.
The mouse model compares intestinal permeability and pathological tissue outcomes. Motility and intestinal specimens differ from clinical drooling and the experiment does not administer figs.
Autoimmune encephalitis review describes neurologic and orofacial signs in antibody-associated syndromes. Figures and treatment review give no Parkinson food comparison.
The original study proposes a motor rating for a porcine parkinsonism model and reports Figure 1 for the one animal available for longitudinal scoring. It gives no raw fig or drooling effect.
Erythropoietin pilot in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis reports functional, strength and safety observations. Drug administration and pooled functional measures supply no raw-fig comparison.
Head and neck therapy review distinguishes different causes of excess saliva and reports salivary-gland treatment literature. It supplies clinical drooling context without a culinary comparison.
Table 4 reports separate Japanese and English distributions for the combined item 2.2 Saliva and drooling. This is scale validation using cohort distributions, without a tested fig exposure.
Cannabinoid evidence review describes other plant-derived compounds. The salivary symptom mention concerns ALS self-reports, outside the frozen ingredient and Parkinson comparison.
The public human clinical table records drooling in one donor described as having parkinsonism with Lewy body disease. This is symptom history with no diet comparison.
The clinical review describes an antipsychotic-associated emergency syndrome. Its autonomic signs, rigidity and illustrated diagnostic context do not involve tested raw figs.
Parkinson drumming pilot tests an activity intervention and reports overall quality of life and motor scores. Fig terms refer to illustrations; no separate drooling or fig-exposure result is given.

Dopa-responsive dystonia review describes drooling or salivary symptoms with inherited monoamine disorders. These heterogeneous phenotypes and medicine comparisons provide differential context without a fig intervention.
SCA3 swallowing study uses videofluoroscopy and swallowing scales. Drooling is described as a symptom in background literature; figures present clinical screening performance and do not test fig.
The PKAN imaging article lists drooling in individual disease histories. Its comparison uses brain imaging by mutation status, without a raw fig or salivation intervention.

Historical review describes qualitative changes in drooling after harmala-containing preparations in earlier parkinsonism series, including postencephalitic patients. Those botanical exposures differ from figs and historical comparisons are uncontrolled.

Printed pages 692–696 describe presentation and diagnostic delay in Wilson disease. Drooling and dysarthria enter the clinical histories, with no Parkinson fig comparison.
The 21-page review covers motor patterns of childhood cerebral palsy. Its figures describe motor and lesion findings. No Parkinson drooling estimate or culinary fig intervention.

The seven-page clinical paper describes injected botulinum treatment for focal dystonia and hemifacial spasm. Its figure and swallowing safety contexts do not establish a raw fig and Parkinson drooling comparison.

The three-page motor-system review lists drooling among associated manifestations of parkinsonism. It discusses medical and physiotherapy context with no isolated fig intervention.

All six pages document a pediatric case of striatopallidonigral degeneration. The report describes salivary drooling in the neurological course and shows tissue illustrations, without a raw-fig comparison.
